Oceans cover most of our planet and conceal many secrets beneath 
their waters. Have you ever wondered what the land under the 
oceans looks like, why ocean water is always moving, or what wealth 
and resources lie beneath the sea? How do areas like maritime zones 
help countries use the oceans, and how can we protect ourselves 
from ocean hazards, such as cyclones and tsunamis? 
In this chapter, we will explore these human–ocean connections 
and discover how oceans shape both our daily lives and the world 
around us.
Ocean Relief
As we explore human–ocean connections, let us begin with the 
ocean floor and its features. Just as land has mountains, valleys, and 
plains, the ocean floor, too, has several landforms, together known 
as submarine relief or ocean relief. These include underwater 
mountains, valleys, plateaus, and trenches. The Mariana Trench 
in the Pacific Ocean is the deepest place on Earth, while the 
Mid-Ocean Ridge is the world’s longest mountain range, hidden 
beneath the ocean. Some underwater mountains like Mauna Kea 
(Hawai‘i) are even taller than Mount Everest.

Movement of Ocean Water—Waves, 
Tides, and Currents
The water in the oceans is constantly in motion. Waves, tides, and 
currents are not merely movements of ocean water; they help shape 
the Earth’s surface, support marine life, aid fishing and travel, 
and even influence climate. Let us learn more about these oceanic 
movements.
Waves
When the surface of the ocean rises and falls alternately, it is called 
a wave. Waves are primarily caused by winds blowing across the 
water. They carry energy across the oceans over long distances. 
Observe Fig. 1.3 and note the crests (high peaks) and troughs (lower 
valleys). 
Waves are often called coastal architects as they shape the shoreline 
through erosion and sediment transport. Observe the various 
landforms formed by waves in Fig. 1.4 and note how wave action 
creates erosional features, such as sea cracks, caves, arches, sea stacks, 
and stumps. Also notice the original headland shown in the figure. 
In addition to erosional landforms, waves also form depositional 
features such as beaches.

During storms, strong winds can generate huge waves that may 
cause significant damage along coastlines. The giant waves majorly 
caused by underwater earthquakes are called tsunamis, which can 
be extremely destructive. On reaching the shore, tsunamis may attain 
a maximum vertical height above sea level, known as the run-up 
height, of up to 30 metres, or even more in extreme cases. 
Tides
Tides are the rhythmic rise and fall of ocean water that occur 
twice a day in most parts of the world. When the water rises to 
its highest level and covers much of the shore, it is called high tide 
(flood tide). When the water falls to its lowest level and moves 
away from the shore, it is called low tide (ebb tide). Observe Fig. 1.5 
and note the change in water level during high and low tides. Do 
you notice the oval layer around the Earth indicating water level? 
Can you also see how the water level rises during high tide and falls 
during low tide?

High tides are important for navigation because they raise the water 
level near the shore, allowing ships to enter harbours more easily. 
In ports and coastal areas, tidal information is essential, as tidal 
ranges in some ports can reach 4–5 metres. The Gulf of Khambhat 
has one of the highest tidal ranges, at about 12 metres. Before a ship 
berths at a port, it must check both the water depth and the tidal 
range to ensure safe docking, especially during low tide.
Some sea channels, such as the Singapore Strait, contain shallow 
areas. Hence, ships such as Very Large Crude Carriers (VLCCs) 
passing through these regions often wait for hours to transit only 
during high tide to ensure sufficient water depth and avoid running 
aground.
Tidal changes also generate strong currents because large volumes 
of water flow in and out of coastal areas. These tidal currents can 
reach speeds of 5–6 knots (about 9–11 km/h).

High tides also support fishing activities (Fig. 1.7). During high tide, 
many fish move closer to the shore in search of food and shelter, 
enabling fishing communities to obtain a better catch.
The rise and fall of tidal water are also used to generate electricity 
in some places (Fig. 1.8). India has a vast coastline of 11,098.81 
kilometres, and although tidal energy is not yet widely used on a 
large scale, certain areas have been identified as suitable for its 
development. The Gulf of Kutch, the Gulf of Khambhat, and the 
Sundarbans are among the major tidal energy sites in India.

Ocean Currents
Ocean currents are continuous streams of water that flow across 
the ocean surface in definite directions (Fig. 1.9). They are caused 
by factors, such as winds, the Earth’s rotation (Coriolis force), 
differences in temperature and salinity, and the shape of continents 
and ocean basins. Ocean currents may be warm or cold depending 
on the direction from which the water flows. Currents flowing from 
warmer regions are called warm currents, while those flowing from 
colder regions are called cold currents. On maps, warm currents are 
usually shown in red and cold currents in blue. 
THINK ABOUT IT
Observe the map carefully and note the movement patterns of 
cold and warm currents. Do you think these currents affect the 
temperature of nearby coastal regions?
The Gulf Stream, a warm current originating in the Gulf of Mexico 
in the Atlantic Ocean, flows towards Norway and keeps its waters 
relatively warm. As a result, sea ice does not form easily in the 
Norwegian region despite its high latitude (60°–70°). In contrast, 
the Labrador Current, a cold current flowing along the east coast of 
Canada, carries freezing water and supports the formation of sea ice 
and icebergs even at lower latitudes.

Cyclones and Tsunamis—Early Warning 
Systems
Oceans and seas can give rise to sudden natural hazards such as 
cyclones, which are large rotating storms, and tsunamis, which are 
giant waves caused by earthquakes. To protect people from such 
dangers, scientists have developed Early Warning Systems that work 
like giant alarm systems for coastal areas. To reduce risks, people, 
communities, and governments must act in advance. Early Warning 
Systems help detect cyclones and tsunamis, predict disasters, and 
issue timely warnings so that people can evacuate and stay safe.

India has several Cyclone Warning Services and Marine Weather 
Services that monitor storms along both the eastern and western 
coasts. For early warning systems to be effective, they must function 
continuously. India uses advanced technologies to predict cyclones 
at an early stage, which has significantly reduced the loss of human 
and animal lives.
The Government of India has launched the National Cyclone Risk 
Mitigation Project (NCRMP) to build cyclone shelters, strengthen 
warning systems, and improve emergency response mechanisms. 
The project focuses on cyclone-prone States and Union Territories and 
includes a Decision Support System (DSS) for disaster management 
authorities. The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information 
Services (INCOIS), in collaboration with the India Meteorological 
Department (IMD), has also established the Storm Surge Early 
Warning System (SSEWS) for the Indian coasts. Its main objective is 
to protect coastal communities by forecasting cyclone-induced storm 
surges and the extent of coastal inundation.

For an early warning system to save lives, information must reach 
the public quickly and effectively. The Indian Tsunami Early Warning 
Centre (ITEWC) is tasked with sending alerts to the Government 
of India, which then informs state governments and emergency 
response teams. Reliable communication is ensured through 
satellite-based communication networks, SMS, emails, and coastal 
display boards. 
Besides technology, public awareness and training programmes are 
equally important for an effective early warning system. Educating 
officials and coastal communities on how to interpret warnings helps 
ensure that when disasters such as cyclones are predicted, people 
know how to respond appropriately.

Marine Resources and Their Significance
Do you recall learning about natural resources in the Grade 8 Social 
Science Part 1 textbook? These resources are obtained from land, 
water, forests and animals, and other natural sources. Oceans, too, 
are vast storehouses of resources, and the materials and features 
found in oceans that have intrinsic or economic value are called 
marine resources. Marine resources can be broadly classified into 
two categories—Marine Living Resources and Marine Non-living 
Resources. They include fish and seafood, biodiversity, oil and 
natural gas, minerals, sand and gravel, renewable blue energy 
sources such as tidal and wave energy, tourism potential, and 
unique ecosystems such as coral reefs. Fig. 1.17 presents a detailed 
classification of marine resources. 
Significance of Marine Resources
Marine resources are vital for food security, economic activities, and 
maintaining a healthy environment (Fig. 1.17). Countries with long 
coastlines, such as India, benefit greatly from the sea. Fishing, trade, 
and tourism provide livelihoods to millions of people, while oceans 
also support biodiversity and sustain numerous plant and animal 
species. However, marine resources must be used responsibly 
without disturbing marine ecosystems.

Maritime Zones
Have you ever wondered who owns the oceans and how 
countries decide where they can fish or travel? To understand this, 
we need to learn about maritime zones—different areas of the ocean 
defined by international law.
The sea area closest to a country is called its territorial waters, over 
which the country has near-complete control, subject to the right of 
innocent passage for foreign ships. Just as on land, the government 
can make laws relating to customs, immigration, and pollution 
control in this zone.
Observe Fig. 1.20 and note the extent of the territorial sea in nautical 
miles. Beyond this lies the contiguous zone, extending from the 
baseline up to 24 nautical miles, where the country has limited 
control over customs, fiscal matters, and illegal immigration.

Innocent Passage is a principle that allows foreign ships to pass 
through the territorial waters of a country as long as they do 
not threaten its peace, good order, or security. Ships must move 
continuously without stopping, except in emergencies or cases of 
breakdowns. This right does not permit activities such as fishing, 
military operations, or other non-peaceful actions.
Beyond the contiguous zone, lie the Exclusive Economic Zones 
(EEZs), which extend from the baseline up to 200 nautical miles from 
the coast, and are defined under the United Nations Convention on 
the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) by global agreement. In these zones, a 
country has special rights to use ocean resources, such as fish, oil, 
and gas, although ships from other countries may still pass through 
peacefully. It is important to note, however, that the country does not 
fully own or control the waters of the EEZ. 
Beyond the EEZs of all countries lie the high seas, also known as 
international waters. Covering about 64 per cent of the world’s 
oceans, these waters do not belong to any single country and are 
therefore considered part of the global commons. All countries enjoy 
equal rights on the high seas, including navigation, fishing, flying 
over them, laying undersea cables, building lawful structures such 
as artificial lands, and exploring for minerals.

Although the high seas are essential, they also present many 
challenges. Since no single country controls them, issues, such 
as overfishing, illegal fishing, and conflicts over resources often 
arise. These problems affect millions of people who depend on 
the sea for food and livelihoods. Ensuring navigation and safety is 
also more difficult without clear enforcement mechanisms. On the 
high seas, the laws of the flag state—the country in which a ship is 
registered—apply. 
International Maritime Rules and Regulations
In the earlier sections of this chapter, you learnt that oceans are 
vital for trade, travel, and communication. To ensure that activities 
at sea remain safe, fair, and peaceful, countries follow a set of 
international rules and agreements known as maritime law or 
maritime regulations. These laws regulate how ships operate and 
move; protect the marine environment; address issues such as 
piracy, terrorism, natural disasters, and accidents; safeguard trade 
routes; and help settle disputes between countries.
LET’S EXPLORE
Maritime disputes are conflicts or disagreements between 
countries over territory, resources, or rights in naval areas such as 
oceans, seas, or coastal regions. Can you find out some countries 
that have conflicts over their territorial sea waters?
Important Maritime Rules and Regulations
Just as there are traffic rules on land, ships must follow “rules of 
the road at sea” to avoid accidents. These rules, known as COLREGs 
(Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing 
Collisions at Sea), include maintaining a proper lookout, deciding 
which side to pass on, identifying the give-way and stand-on vessels, 
proceeding at a safe speed, and using lights, sound signals, shapes 
(for different types of vessels such as fishing boats), along with 
appropriate actions to prevent collisions. In addition, ships use 
international signals and radio communication to share information 
and prevent accidents, especially in crowded or hazardous waters.

Ships must also meet safety standards and are prohibited from 
polluting the seas. The MARPOL (International Convention for the 
Prevention of Pollution from Ships) Convention is an important 
international agreement aimed at reducing pollution from ships. 
Why are Maritime Rules Important?
International maritime rules, regulations, and agreements help keep 
the oceans safe and ensure the fair and sustainable use of ocean 
resources. These rules enable countries to cooperate in using marine 
resources without conflict while protecting marine life, ships, sailors, 
and coastal communities. Without such regulations, the oceans could 
become dangerous and chaotic, with increased pollution, accidents, 
collisions, and disputes over resources. By establishing common 
standards for all ships, regardless of the country they belong to, 
maritime rules help keep the oceans safe, clean, and open for trade 
and travel.

Geography helps us understand how climate, landforms, and water 
shape life on Earth—and how humans adapt their lives to these 
conditions. From forests and grasslands to deserts and coastal

the same time, human activities influence these natural systems 
in significant ways. This chapter explores the close relationships 
among physical features, climate, and living organisms, and 
encourages us to reflect on our responsibility towards preserving 
the diversity of life on Earth.

Terrestrial Biomes
Terrestrial biomes are classified into forests, grasslands, deserts, and 
tundra, based on their climate.
Forest Biome
A forest biome is like nature’s giant green umbrella—warm, wet, and 
bursting with life at every level, from the tallest trees to the damp 
forest floor. Tropical rainforests are mainly found near the Equator, 
between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn (23.5° N 
to 23.5° S). These regions remain hot and wet throughout the year, 
which supports the growth of dense forests. The largest tropical 
rainforests are located in the Amazon Basin in South America, the 
Congo Basin in Africa, and parts of Southeast Asia, such as Indonesia 
and Malaysia. Smaller rainforest regions are also found in Central 
America, as well as in India’s Andaman & Nicobar Islands, and the 
Northeastern states. Together, these areas form the world’s richest 
storehouse of biodiversity with rich genetic resources. They preserve 
unique genetic material, supporting conservation and scientific 
research, and are hence also known as a ‘gene bank’. Forests also 
play an important role in maintaining oxygen levels and balancing 
the Earth’s climate.

Desert Biome
Deserts are the driest biomes, receiving very little rainfall. They can 
be hot, like the Sahara in Africa, or cold, like the Gobi in Asia. The 
Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is one of the world’s largest salt deserts,

make it difficult for life to survive; however, plants like cacti and 
animals such as camels, lizards, and snakes are specially adapted 
to these conditions. They can store water and withstand heat and 
dryness. Deserts often have sandy soil and sparse vegetation. Despite 
their harshness, they are home to unique ecosystems, and many of 
them also provide valuable resources such as minerals and oil.

Tundra Biome
The tundra biome is the coldest of all and is found near the Arctic 
and Antarctic regions. It has very long, harsh winters and short 
summers. The soil is frozen almost year-round—a condition called 
permafrost—which makes it difficult for trees to grow. The 
vegetation is limited to mosses, lichens, and small shrubs. And 
animals, such as reindeer, arctic foxes, and polar bears, which are 
well adapted to survive freezing temperatures, are often found here. 
The tundra is fragile, and even small temperature changes can affect 
its ecosystem.

Interconnectedness between Biomes 
and Living Beings
Biomes are closely connected to living beings because they provide 
a natural environment where plants, animals, and humans can 
survive and interact. At the same time, living beings also influence 
biomes—animals help in pollination and seed dispersal, humans 
modify landscapes for farming or cities, and microorganisms recycle 
nutrients. In this way, biomes and living beings are interconnected 
systems that depend on one another to maintain ecological balance 
and biodiversity. We will discuss some of the aspects of this 
interconnectedness in the following section.
Maintaining Ecological Balance and Biodiversity
Biodiversity
Biodiversity is the variety of life on Earth, 
including plants, animals, microorganisms, 
and the ecosystems they inhabit (Fig. 2.11). 
It refers not only to the number of different 
species but also to the genetic differences 
within species and the variety of habitats 
and ecological processes that sustain life. 
In simple terms, biodiversity means the 
richness of life forms and the natural 
balance they create, which is essential 
for maintaining healthy ecosystems and 
supporting human survival.

The geographical aspects of biodiversity conservation focus on 
how location, climate, landforms, and ecosystems influence the 
protection and management of living organisms. Since biodiversity 
is unevenly distributed across the Earth, geography plays a vital role 
in conservation. Some key aspects of conservation are—
Hotspots of Biodiversity: Certain regions, such as the Himalaya, 
the Western Ghats, the North–East India, and the Andaman & Nicobar 
Islands, are rich in unique species found nowhere else. Identifying 
and protecting these hotspots is a priority in conservation.
Ecosystem-Based Conservation: Different biomes (forests, wetlands, 
deserts, coasts, and mountains) support distinct life forms. Conservation 
strategies must suit the geographical setting; for example, mangrove 
protection along coasts or afforestation in mountains.
Protected Areas: National parks, wildlife sanctuaries, biosphere 
reserves, and World Heritage Sites are chosen based on geography 
to preserve critical habitats and prevent habitat fragmentation.
Geographical Barriers and Corridors: Natural features like rivers, 
mountains, and valleys serve as barriers or corridors that influence 
animal movement and gene flow. Conservation planning uses this 
knowledge to create wildlife corridors.
Human–Environment Interaction: Geography also considers 
how local communities use land, water, and forests. Sustainable 
practices vary with geography, such as terrace farming in the hills or 
agroforestry in the plains.
In short, biodiversity conservation is an intrinsic part of geography 
because the survival of species depends on their location, habitat 
conditions, and human activity within those regions.

Forest Ecotourism
Ecotourism in forests refers to responsible travel to forested areas 
where tourists enjoy nature while contributing to its conservation. 
Forests are home to a wide variety of plants, animals, rivers, and

learning about ecosystems. For example, visiting national parks, 
wildlife sanctuaries, or trekking through rainforests allows visitors 
to observe biodiversity while supporting conservation programmes 
and generating income for the local people. Thus, ecotourism in

sustainable development.

Challenges Faced by People Living in Forests
People living in forests often struggle to access essential facilities 
such as healthcare, education, and clean water. Women are 
exposed to fuelwood fumes and face, many health issues, making 
their daily lives difficult. Forest dwellers depend heavily on forest 
produce such as firewood, honey, bamboo, and medicinal plants 
for their livelihood. Restrictions on forest use, deforestation, and 
the commercial exploitation of resources often limit their access to 
these resources. This creates a conflict between conservation laws 
and their survival needs, leading to economic insecurity.
Forested hilly regions are prone to natural disasters such as floods 
and landslides. Floods can wash away homes, crops, and roads, while 
landslides can bury villages and cut off access to essential services. 
Forest fires can quickly spread through dense vegetation, destroying 
homes and resources. Human care and preventive measures can 
help prevent many forest fires. 
Crops are often damaged by elephants, monkeys, or wild boars, and 
sometimes people face direct attacks. Such conflicts not only cause 
economic losses but also create fear and insecurity among forest 
communities.
Many forest dwellers also face discrimination and neglect from 
mainstream society. They are often engaged in selling forest 
products at relatively low prices. Therefore, creating opportunities 
for processing and marketing these products is essential to 
enhance their income. Forest communities also require assistance 
in accessing government schemes and programmes, as well as 
greater awareness of their legal rights.

Mendha Lekha: A Case Study in Community Forest 
Management
Mendha Lekha is a small tribal village located in the Gadchiroli 
district of Maharashtra, known for its effective community-
based forest management and self-governance. The village, 
inhabited mainly by the Gond tribe, became the first in India 
to gain rights over its forest resources under the Forest Rights 
Act (2006). The people of Mendha Lekha follow the principle of 
Mawa Nate Mawa Raj (our village, our rule), ensuring that all 
decisions are made collectively through the Gram Sabha. They 
protect and sustainably utilise their 1,800 hectares of forest by 
regulating tree cutting, preventing forest fires, and promoting bamboo 
harvesting as a renewable resource. The revenue from the forest 
produce is used for community welfare activities such as education 
and infrastructure. This also upholds the fundamental rights of 
the people to participate in governance and control resources that 
sustain their livelihoods. Simultaneously, the villagers fulfil their 
fundamental duties by protecting biodiversity and preventing illegal 
exploitation. This model has not only strengthened local livelihoods 
but also demonstrates how traditional knowledge, rights, and duties, 
as well as democratic participation, can coexist to achieve sustainable 
forest conservation (Fig. 2.22).

Ecological Commons—Shared Resources
The term ecological commons refer to natural resources like 
forests, rivers, lakes, grazing lands, air, and biodiversity that are 
shared by a community and used collectively for its survival and 
well-being. Unlike private property, these resources are not owned 
by any single individual but belong to the community as a whole, 
and are often managed through traditional rules and practices. 
For centuries, people have depended on the ecological commons 
for food, water, fuel, fodder, and medicinal plants. However, with 
population growth, industrial use, and privatisation, many of 
these commons are shrinking or degrading. Protecting ecological 
commons is important not only for the livelihoods of rural and tribal 
communities but also for maintaining ecological balance, regulating 
climate, and conserving biodiversity.
A Case Study of Commons-based Fisheries 
Management in Bihar
After independence, The Indian Fisheries Act, 1897, remained the 
basis for the governance of inland fisheries. Historically, control 
over perennial water bodies and diara waterfronts in Bihar was 
held by large landowners who marginalised the fishing community, 
rendering them the most vulnerable group in an environment 
abundant with aquatic resources.

Chapter 3
The period between 1000 CE and 1700 CE witnessed profound 
political, social, and cultural changes. The Indian subcontinent 
experienced repeated invasions and wars accompanied by religious 
discrimination and social distress. Regional powers frequently 
resisted invaders who were making inroads into their territories. 
This resistance took both military and cultural forms. Nonetheless, 
this period manifested the resilience of the Indian civilisation, 
which safeguarded its core ideas and values. Indian society not 
only defended itself from external threats but also preserved its 
traditions. In this chapter, we will see how resistance and resilience 
shaped this period of Indian history.
Let us begin by understanding the meaning of resistance and 
resilience in the context of the period under study and how they are 
interconnected.
Resilience refers to the capacity to, survive and adapt in challenging 
situations, including times of political unrest and instability. It is also 
about how communities and groups across diverse regions respond 
to challenges and opportunities. This capacity to absorb and adapt 
to hardship while preserving inherited socio-cultural and spiritual 
traditions can also be understood as resilience. The idea of India’s 
resilient spirit extends beyond political and military spheres.

Rajput Dynasties: Confederacies and 
Resistance (1200–1500 CE)
The establishment of the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 was a turning 
point in Indian history. The new state introduced administrative 
practices that led to greater centralisation of authority. For example, 
the iqta system, under which territories were assigned to military 
commanders in lieu of salaries, became a mechanism for land 
revenue collection and a system that increased the burden on 
the peasantry. Furthermore, during their military campaigns for 
territorial expansion, the forces of the Sultanate demolished sites 
sacred to the local communities. This led to stiff resistance from 
several kingdoms and chieftains. Therefore, resistance throughout 
the Delhi Sultanate was fuelled by both political factors and the 
determination to preserve socio-cultural continuity. For instance, 
the Yādava dynasty of western Deccan (Devagiri), several Rajput 
dynasties of present-day Rajasthan, the Kākatīya rulers of eastern 
Deccan (Warangal), and the Hoysālas of present-day Karnataka 
repeatedly resisted the Sultans of Delhi. These states played an 
important role in checking the expansion of the Sultanate.
Over the years and under different Sultans, the Delhi Sultanate 
faced opposition and defiance from several states and regions 
including Mewar, Gwalior, Malwa, Awadh, Etawah, Ajmer, Jalore, 
Kalinjar, and Kannauj.

Rajput–Mughal Dynamics: Politics and 
Complexities of Rule (1500–1700 CE)
In the early 1500s, the weakening and subsequent decline of the 
Delhi Sultanate under its last ruler, Ibrāhim Lodī, opened the door 
to two parallel developments. First, Zahiruddin Muhammad, also 
known as Bābur, from Central Asia launched an invasion on India. 
Second, Indian rulers began to assert their own authority. In 1526, 
Bābur defeated the Lodi forces in the First Battle of Panipat, bringing 
the Sultanate to an end. In 1527, Rāṇā Sangrām Singh I, popularly 
known as Rāṇā Sāngā, of Mewar led a Rajput confederacy against 
Bābur in the Battle of Khanua. The battle ended in favour of Bābur 
and is seen as an important turning point in Indian history.
As Mughal rule consolidated its power, relations between the 
Rajputs and the Mughals evolved over time, shaped by strategic 
considerations. Some Rajput kingdoms such as Mewar, maintained 
stiff resistance to Mughal authority, while others like the Kachhwāha 
Rajputs of Amber, negotiated cooperative relationships. The 
Mughals, for their part, had a strong incentive to collaborate with 
the Rajputs—they needed the Rajputs’ military might, their loyalty as 
well as their administrative strength to consolidate and stabilise the 
Mughal Empire. Towards this end, the Mughals integrated some of 
the Rajputs into the empire through the grant of mansabs and other 
understandings.

successfully defended their territories against Mughal invasion.

Vijayanagara Empire: Resilience 
against Expansion 
Resistance to foreign invasions was not confined to northern India. 
In the Deccan and beyond, the expanding campaigns of the Delhi 
Sultanate steadily weakened the older kingdoms of the south. Malik 
Kāfūr, Alauddin Khiljī’s general, attacked major cities and temples, 
including those at Warangal, Belur, and Madurai. Later, Muhammad 
bin Tughlaq’s rise to power extended the Sultanate’s influence even 
farther south, ultimately contributing to the decline of the Pandya 
Kingdom and the eventual emergence of a new sultanate territory 
known as the Madurai Sultanate. 
It was against this backdrop that the Vijayanagara Empire rose 
in 1336 to check the expansion of the Sultanate into peninsular 
India. Harihara and Bukkā established the independent kingdom of 
Vijayanagara—meaning ‘City of Victory’—located near present-day 
Hampi, Karnataka. The region’s geography, including a formidable 
river and rugged, rocky terrain, provided Vijayanagara with a strong 
natural defence and a secure base for military operations. They 
made determined efforts to defend and expand their state’s frontiers. 
The empire gradually expanded by annexing territory south of the 
Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers and became one of the richest and 
most influential states, encouraging the flourishing of literature in 
Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, and Sanskrit. Vijayanagara’s capital city 
became a centre of trade, culture, and political power in southern 
India.
During Bukkā’s reign, Vijayanagara made major territorial gains, 
including the subjugation of the Madurai Sultanate and the 
annexation of Arcot. In 1342, the ageing Hoysāla king Vīra Ballāla III

Due to the growing socio-cultural influence of the Sikh Gurus, the

turning point in the history of the Sikhs and contributed to a gradual

The brutality of the Mughal state against the Sikh Gurus particularly

the Gurus for the cause of the faith became the defining features of

martyrdom of the Sikh Gurus to uphold their faith and principles firmed

During the 17th century, the Jats, a farming community from Ganga–
Yamuna Doab were burdened with heavy taxes and exploitation by

religious policies led to growing resentment amongst the Jats. In

Mughal Empire. Mughal forces struggled for many months to suppress 
the uprising.

advantage of Aurangzeb’s prolonged military campaigns in the Deccan 
and rebelled once again under the leadership of the zamindars of 
Sinsani and Sogar. The Mughals sent several armies to suppress the 
rebellion, leading to a long and fierce struggle in which both sides 
suffered heavy losses. By 1691, the Mughals had gained the upper hand.

Temples: The Resilience of Sacred Sites
Temples functioned as central pillars of the region’s socio-economic 
and political life. These religious institutions evolved into major 
economic hubs that managed extensive land grants, provided 
employment to hundreds of specialised workers, and served as 
financial institutions for local traders. Rulers used temple patronage 
to strengthen their political legitimacy. Beyond their spiritual and 
religious functions, temples facilitated social integration and served 
as centres of education and culture, where artistic traditions such 
as Bharatanatyam and many other art forms were preserved. They 
also exercised quasi-judicial authority, collecting local taxes and 
administering legal penalties.
Temples also served as sources of legitimacy for political authority. 
The deities of these temples were regarded as protectors of the state 
and its people. In some cases, the deity was regarded as the ruler, 
while the actual ruler governed as the deity’s deputy. For example, 
the Gajapati rulers of Odisha called themselves the Rauta (deputy) 
of Jagannath. Similarly, the Kachhwāhā rulers of Jaipur governed on 
behalf of Govindadevajī, while the Rajput rulers of Kota regarded 
themselves as representatives of Rāma.
Temples in India also functioned as significant economic 
institutions. They provided employment to a wide range of groups, 
including architects, artisans, sculptors, priests, musicians, and 
administrative staff. As substantial landholders, temples received 
donations, endowments, and land grants, often given as acts of

The main source of state income was land revenue, and the 
expanding frontiers of empires resulted in an increase in the 
area under cultivation. Over time, the collection of land revenue 
became increasingly strict and exploitative at various levels of 
administration. For example, during the reigns of Alauddin Khiljī 
and Mohammad bin Tughlaq, the land tax was raised to as much 
as 50 per cent of total agricultural production, in addition to other 
taxes. Moreover, the Sultans of Delhi, and later the Mughals had 
limited role in maritime trade. Their concerns regarding coastal 
areas and port cities were largely confined to political and military 
matters and, to some extent, the collection of customs duties. As a 
result, coastal areas and their commerce remained largely in the 
hands of regional power holders and local communities.
Irrigation technologies such as rope pulleys, spinning wheel, and 
Persian wheel were widely used by local populations, resulting in 
enhanced agricultural and economic output. In the Vijayanagara 
Empire, agricultural production varied greatly in both form and 
scale. Consequently, irrigation systems ranged from extensive canal 
networks to small rain-fed patches of land. A defining feature of the 
Vijayanagara economy was its investment in small-scale irrigation.

The terms ‘government’ and ‘governance’ are closely related. 
However, they are not synonymous. Government refers to the 
institutions and authorities that exercise political power, while 
governance refers to the process by which decisions are made, 
implemented, and monitored in the public interest. The government 
formulates and implements people-centric policies, and good 
governance ensures that these policies are transparent, accountable, 
effective, and responsive to people’s needs. Governance is the system 
through which decisions are made, implemented, and monitored for 
the welfare of the people. It refers to the way a country, state, city, 
village, school, or organisation is managed. Therefore, understanding 
governance is essential to know how government impacts our lives.

Evolution of Governance in India
In the previous section, we studied that while the government is 
the institutional aspect, governance refers to its functional aspect. 
The government’s institutional setup influences the nature of 
governance, and governance initiatives, in turn, require institutional 
adaptations to implement policies and schemes.
We are familiar with the structure of government at different levels 
in India. But the same structure has not always existed as it does 
now; it has evolved from certain historical experiences. Let us 
understand this historical context by looking at the ‘big picture’ of 
the world history. 
Do you remember the phenomenon of colonialism that you learnt 
about in Grade 8? We know that European powers colonised many 
societies, particularly those in Asia, Africa, and the Americas. 
Before colonial rulers forced their own models of governance 
and policy-making on colonised people, these societies governed 
themselves in accordance with local and organic systems. Although 
most colonies had become independent by the end of the 20th 
century, colonial institutions largely persisted, and their structures 
continued to dominate even in contemporary times. India is not 
an exception to the historical legacy of colonialism. However, India 
stands out in two important ways. Firstly, unlike many societies that 
experienced colonial rule, India has preserved most of its knowledge 
of its pre-colonial institutions and traditions of governance through 
texts and practices. Secondly, after Independence in 1947, it was not 
possible to replace all colonial institutions at once. The leaders of 
independent India therefore framed the Constitution in the spirit of 
India’s own values and ideals.
Since Independence, Indian institutions have continued to draw upon 
traditional ideas and values of governance and have adapted them 
to the needs of a modern democracy. For example, the British ‘Order 
of the Star of India’ used the phrase, ‘Heaven’s Light, Our Guide’ as 
its motto but after Independence, we have adopted ‘Satyamev Jayate’

us cross safely, the clean drinking water supplied to our homes, the 
electricity that lights our classrooms, the public parks where we play,

healthcare, transportation, sanitation, environmental protection,

Public policy is about responding to the needs and aspirations of 
the people. Therefore, people play an important role in shaping 
them. People identify issues, express their concerns, participate in 
consultations, provide suggestions, and share feedback after a policy 
is implemented. Governments use this feedback to improve policies

The Making of a Public Policy
A public policy is developed through a systematic process rather 
than a single decision. It usually begins when citizens, government 
officials, researchers, or civil society organisations realise that a 
new need has to be met, an existing problem has to be resolved, or 
a facility has to be made better in the interest of the people. Then 
the government studies the issue, collects information, and consults 
experts, stakeholders, and the public to understand different 
viewpoints and possible solutions. Based on these discussions, 
the government authorities prepare, review, and approve a draft 
policy. Once the policy is approved by the concerned authorities, 
it is translated into programmes and schemes, which provide a 
clear framework for different ministries, departments, and local 
governments to take specific action. The implementation of any 
policy is continuously monitored and evaluated to assess whether 
it is achieving its objectives. Feedback from citizens and other 
stakeholders is used to improve the policy over time. Thus, public 
policy is a continuous cycle of problem identification, consultation, 
policy formulation, implementation, monitoring, evaluation, and 
improvement. This process helps the government respond effectively 
to the changing needs of society.

a) Fixed Deposits (FDs)
Fixed deposits are among the most common and safest investment 
options offered by banks and post offices. In a fixed deposit, a 
person deposits a lump sum amount for a fixed period, such as one,

throughout the investment period. Fixed deposits offer assured 
returns and are suitable for people who prefer safety over high 
returns. 
Other government-backed investment options include the Public

b) Bonds
Bonds are investments through which people lend money to the 
government or companies (issuers of bonds) for a fixed period. 
Bondholders earn regular interest. For example, if you buy a bond 
worth ₹10,000 that pays 5% interest per year, you will receive ₹500 
as interest after one year. If the bond matures after one year, you 
will receive ₹10,500 in total. In reality, the maturity period ranges 
from 1 day to 30 years or more. You may also be able to sell the 
bond before maturity if you need the money earlier, making them 
more liquid. Government bonds are generally considered safer 
than corporate bonds and are suitable for those seeking a stable, 
predictable income.

Protection and Risk Management
Life is full of uncertainties, such as illness, accidents, loss of 
income, or damage to property. These unexpected events 
can lead to significant financial losses. Therefore, an important 
aspect of personal finance is protection—safeguarding your income, 
savings, and assets against such risks.
Insurance
One of the most effective ways to achieve financial protection 
is through insurance. Insurance is a legal contract in which an 
individual pays a regular amount, called a premium, to an insurance 
company. In return, the company agrees to provide financial 
compensation for specific losses or expenses covered under the 
policy. For example, a family may pay ₹500 every month for health 
insurance. If a family member requires medical treatment, the 
insurance company covers a large part of the hospital expenses. 
Without insurance, the family might have to use a substantial portion 
of its savings for the expenses incurred towards the treatment. 
Insurance works on the principle of risk sharing. Many people pay 
premiums into a common pool. In case of any unexpected loss,

Taxes 
Taxes are compulsory payments made by individuals and businesses 
to the government to fund public services, such as schools, hospitals, 
transport, defence, and other essential facilities. There are two main 
types of taxes:
 

Direct taxes, which are paid directly on a person’s or 
organisation’s income or profits, such as the income tax.
 

Indirect taxes, which are added to the price of goods and 
services, such as the Goods and Services Tax (GST). 
Personal Income Tax 
Personal income tax is a tax paid on the income a person earns in a 
year (called a financial year, say 1 April 2001 to 31 March 2002). All 
citizens of India with a personal income are required to pay income 
tax, with the sole exception of individuals who earn below a certain 
limit and are exempt from paying the tax. As income increases, the 
tax payable to the government also increases. This system is known 
as progressive taxation, which aims to reduce income inequality 
by imposing higher tax rates on individuals with higher incomes.

India’s Traditional Entrepreneurial Community
Entrepreneurship in India has deep roots among traditional communities, 
where skills, occupations, and occupational knowledge have been 
passed down through generations. Long before modern startups, these 
communities practised self-employment, innovation, and trade, forming 
the backbone of India’s local economy.
The Chettiar (Nattukottai Chettiar) community from Tamil Nadu 
is a well-known traditional entrepreneurial community. Historically, 
Chettiars were traders, bankers, and moneylenders, operating not only 
across India but also in Sri Lanka, Burma (now Myanmar), Malaysia, and 
other parts of Southeast Asia. They were known for:
 

Strong business ethics and trust-based lending
 

Excellent accounting and record-keeping skills
 

Reinvesting profits into trade, temples, education, and community 
welfare
The Chettiar community built wealth through trade in salt, rice, 
textiles, and finance, often without formal banks. Even today, Chettiar 
entrepreneurship inspires modern India by showing how risk-taking, 
discipline, and long-term vision can build sustainable businesses rooted 
in tradition.
